catalog_locator: ch.5 Tone: p.48 (tone inventory), pp.51-53 (rules 294-295, default tone on toneless verbs and the stress comparison), p.58 (conclusion)
catalog_quote: Lagwan has two contrastive phonological tones, low and high. ... Tone may be either lexical, derivational, grammatical, or may mark a boundary at the end of a phonological phrase. ... (294) Default high tone assignment ... ‘In verbs, toneless syllables of the type #Cə#, #CəC and #CV receive a default high tone.’ ... (295) Default low tone assignment ... ‘Any toneless TBU receives a default low tone.’ ... In many respects the realisation of tone on underlyingly toneless verbs resembles a predictable quantity sensitive stress system: there is no more than one ‘peak’ (high tone) per word; this ‘peak’ is realised at the periphery of the word (in word-initial position) and is attracted to prominent (heavy and tense) syllables. However, in a typical quantity-sensitive stress system, in the absence of the required prominent syllable, a default syllable receives the ‘peak’ instead. This is not …

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (classification tonal-OR-pitch accent) rests on the best and only modern phonological description of Lagwan, Ruff 2005 (SIL Cameroon, 61 pp), which we hold as a text-layer PDF; every fragment of the deciding quotation was found verbatim at pp.48-49, 51-53 and 58, matching the stated locator (one sentence is on p.49 rather than p.48). Ruff describes a two-tone system with no independent word stress; the only stress-like phenomenon (default H on the initial heavy/tense syllable of toneless verbs, otherwise all-L, no default peak) is explicitly analysed as tone and explicitly said not to meet the criteria of a stress system, so the classification follows the source faithfully. Glottolog's remaining descriptive items (Lukas 1936 German grammar, Aboukar 2003 morphology thesis, lexica, a 2007 segmental paper) are older, non-prosodic, or both; no instrumental/prosodic study surf
